headline: Democracy is people deciding together—sharing power rather than concentrating it
universal_truth: When affected people participate in decisions, outcomes better reflect collective needs
fun_facts: The word democracy comes from Greek—'demos' (people) + 'kratos' (power/rule)
Democracy isn't just voting; it includes free speech, press, assembly, and rule of law
Most modern democracies are representative rather than direct
discussion_questions: When is democracy difficult or inefficient?
How do you participate in democratic processes?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Who gets to decide? In autocracy, one person. In oligarchy, a few. In democracy, the people—together. Democracy distributes power, giving everyone a voice in decisions that affect them.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Democracy is slow and messy. Why not just let experts or strong leaders decide?

options.text: Distributed decision-making catches what concentrated power misses—those affected by decisions know things leaders don't; shared power prevents abuse; democracy is slow but resilient
options.response: Yes. No leader knows everything. No expert is accountable the way voters are to themselves. Democracy trades efficiency for wisdom, speed for legitimacy, simplicity for representation.
Voting is part of it, but democracy also protects minorities, ensures rights, and enables participation...

q1.title: More Than Voting
q1.script: Democracy isn't just elections. It includes free speech, free press, independent courts, peaceful assembly. These elements together create democratic society. Voting without these is hollow.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "More Than Voting"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Informed Participation
q2.script: Democracy requires informed citizens. When people don't know issues, democracy degrades. Your participation responsibility includes staying informed on matters you'll decide.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Minority Protection
q3.script: Majority rule alone is tyranny. True democracy protects minority rights even from majority will. The test of democracy is how it treats those outvoted.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: When affected people participate in decisions, outcomes better reflect collective needs. Value the messy process of deciding together.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 333. Tomorrow, we'll explore your voice in decisions—voting. Until then, appreciate the complexity of democratic participation.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Democratic Practice - How Do You Participate?
growTrack.activity: Beyond voting, how do you participate in democracy? Do you stay informed, speak up, contact representatives, attend meetings? Choose one way to strengthen your democratic participation.
